teaser: In 1338, nine rulers had their own meeting room painted with a warning to themselves.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo is a dim interior view of the whole Sala dei Nove, not a reproduction of one fresco. The frescoes occupy only part of the frame and fine details are unreadable, so the lesson has three interactive blocks pointing at large regions. A better image (or one per wall) would allow much more.
Identification of the walls in this photo: center = Allegory of Good Government; right = Effects of Good Government in the City; left = Bad Government. Deduced from what is visible, check.
The cord itself is too thin to see in this photo; the lines block traces its known path approximately.
Peace reclining on a cushion over a pile of armor, olive branch in hand, pose derived from ancient Roman art: standard account.
Street dancing banned by Sienese law: commonly cited, check. The dancers are sometimes argued to be men.
The Nine served two-month terms and lived in the palace during them: check.
Painted February 1338 to May 1339 (payment records).
Signature text: AMBROSIVS LAVRENTII DE SENIS HIC PINXIT VTRINQUE; the lettering band under the central fresco is visible but not legible in the photo.
Ambrogio and Pietro Lorenzetti presumed dead in the plague of 1348; “perhaps half” of Siena's population is an estimate.
Palazzo Pubblico still houses Siena's municipal government.

lesson.text: If you were in charge of a city, what would you put on the walls of the room where you make your decisions? A flag? Portraits of yourselves looking wise? In 1338 the nine men who governed Siena, in central Italy, picked something braver. They ordered a picture of what would happen if they did the job badly.

They were called simply the Nine: merchants and bankers chosen for two months at a time, who lived inside the town hall for their whole term. They hired a local painter, Ambrogio Lorenzetti, to cover three walls of their council room. He worked from early 1338 to the spring of 1339.

That is why you are looking at a photo of a room. This is not one picture but a painted argument that wraps around whoever sits inside it. It is also about politics, with hardly a saint in sight, which was almost unheard of for a work this large in the Middle Ages. Turn your head as a councilor would.

lesson.title: Three walls
lesson.text: One wall states the idea. The other two show the consequences.

spots.title: The idea
spots.text: The end wall is an allegory, a picture in which ideas appear as people. Enthroned figures stand for Justice, Peace and the other qualities a city needs, with a row of citizens below.

spots.title: The good city
spots.text: On the right, a well-run town: tall pink and pale houses stacked up the wall, with tiny figures busy in the streets. Further along, beyond this photo, it opens onto farmed hills.

spots.title: The bad city
spots.text: On the left, the same city under a tyrant, shown with horns and fangs, while Justice lies tied up at his feet. This wall is also the most damaged of the three.

lesson.text: The good city is the famous part. People build, trade, teach, ride out to hunt. It is one of the earliest views of everyday life in a real, recognizable town, and the countryside beside it is among the first true landscapes painted in Europe since ancient Rome.

In the middle of the good city, a ring of dancers moves through the street to the beat of a tambourine. In the real Siena, dancing in the streets was against the law. They are not a snapshot of daily life but a symbol of citizens moving in step.

Back to the end wall, where the theory lives. Two figures are bigger than the rest. On the left, a woman in red on a throne: Justice. On the right, an old bearded king dressed in black and white, the colors of Siena. He is the Common Good, the city itself ruling for everyone. The question is how the two are connected.
Lorenzetti's answer is a piece of string. It is too thin to see in this photo, so here is its route.

lines.label: Down from Justice
lines.text: Cords drop from the scales of Justice to a woman seated beneath her. She is Concord, agreement among citizens, and she twists them into one.

lines.label: Through 24 hands
lines.text: Concord passes the cord to a procession of twenty-four citizens walking in pairs along the bottom. Each one holds it. Nobody pulls.

lines.label: Up to the ruler
lines.text: The cord ends at the wrist of the Common Good. The ruler is literally tied to justice, and the citizens hold the line.

lesson.text: There is a joke buried in it. In Latin, as in English, the word “concord” seems to contain the word “cord”. Lorenzetti turns a pun into a constitution: agreement is the rope that binds power to fairness.
This is among the first great European paintings about how to govern. Its message to the men who paid for it: you are held by a cord, and the people have the other end.
Beside the Common Good sit the virtues, the good qualities of a ruler, lined up on a long patterned bench. Most are upright and alert, some of them armed. One has a completely different attitude.
One figure on the bench is not sitting up straight. Where is she?

spots.title: Peace
spots.text: Dressed in white, she leans back on a cushion with her head propped on one hand. Under the cushion lies a pile of armor she no longer needs. Her lounging pose was borrowed from ancient Roman art.

lesson.text: She gave the room its nickname, the Hall of Peace. And her laziness is the point: peace can only relax like that when justice and the others are doing their work. She is the result, not the effort.
The strip of lettering beneath the end wall includes the painter's signature in Latin. It says that Ambrogio, son of Lorenzo, of Siena, painted here “on both sides”.

The good years did not last. In 1348 the plague known as the Black Death killed perhaps half of Siena. Ambrogio disappears from the records that year, as does his brother Pietro, also a painter, and both are believed to have died in it. In 1355 the Nine were overthrown.

The room survived them all. The building is still Siena's town hall today, and the three walls still make their case to anyone who walks in. Which leaves a question for you: on which wall would you paint the place where you live?

quiz.question: Who commissioned these frescoes?
quiz.explanation: The nine men who ruled Siena had their own council room painted.

quiz.question: What is an allegory?
options: A picture in which ideas appear as people
A painting made on wet plaster
quiz.explanation: Justice, Peace and the Common Good are all ideas shown as human figures.

quiz.question: What links Justice to the Common Good?
options: A cord held by twenty-four citizens
quiz.explanation: The cord runs from the scales of Justice through Concord and the citizens to the ruler's wrist.

quiz.question: How is Peace shown?
options: Reclining in white on a cushion
quiz.explanation: She lounges with her head on her hand, with armor piled under her cushion.

quiz.question: What colors does the Common Good wear?
options: Black and white, the colors of Siena
quiz.explanation: He is dressed in Siena's own colors because he stands for the city.

facts.text: The fresco cycle is mostly about saints and miracles.
facts.explanation: Its subject is politics: what good and bad government do to a city.

facts.text: The dancers in the good city show something that was illegal in real Siena.
facts.explanation: Street dancing was banned, so the dancers are a symbol of harmony.

facts.text: Ambrogio Lorenzetti went on painting in Siena for decades after finishing this room.
facts.explanation: He vanishes from the records in 1348 and is believed to have died in the Black Death.
